name: Les Six Hêtres de Longlou

location.address: A clearing in the Fagne de Longlou (also called Fagne de Tirifaye), in the forest between Xhoffraix and Hockai, north of the Route de l'Ancienne Douane, Beverce, Malmedy

access: Free, in a forest clearing reached by marked trails (the GR56 long-distance trail passes the spot) in the Hautes Fagnes; open at all times, no ticket.
transport: In the forest between Xhoffraix and Hockai near Malmedy; no public transport stop at the site, reached on foot via the GR56 or local walking trails.
story:
Shepherds used to stop here at noon with their flocks, and the beeches they rested under are still standing, though not for much longer. The clearing in the Fagne de Longlou was a prandj'lohe, the local name for a midday resting place, and the spruce plantation that now closes in on every side did not exist when the shepherds used it. They would not recognise the approach.

The beeches are roughly 250 years old by the estimate of the local hiking guides, and Wallonia classified the site as protected heritage on 15 January 1936. The GR56 long-distance trail runs past, which is how most people arrive: on foot, through the Hautes Fagnes, with the clearing appearing only when the conifers open up.

Know what you are walking to. The old trees are at the end of their lives, and in 1993 the Amis des Fagnes planted young beeches beside them so the resting place would outlast its namesakes. How many of the original six still stand is not settled: one account says three, and we have not been able to confirm it. If you have stood in the clearing recently, tell us the count.

What you find is a place in the middle of handing itself over, old trunks and their replacements side by side. That is a reason to go sooner rather than later.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old beeches standing in an open clearing ringed by spruce, with young beeches planted in 1993 beside them. It stands on the GR56 in the Fagne de Longlou.

best_time.label: October, when the old beeches turn copper against the dark spruce

name: The Old Lime of Weywertz

location.address: On the square in front of St. Michael's Church, Lindenstrasse, Weywertz, Butgenbach

access: Free, on the open public square in front of the village church; open at all times, no ticket.
transport: In the centre of Weywertz village, Butgenbach; reachable on foot within the village, exact bus stop not confirmed this pass.
story:
The church behind this lime is the newcomer. St. Michael's was rebuilt in 1959, on the site of earlier churches, while the tree in front of it has stood on the square since 1668.

That date is unusually firm for a village tree. The municipality's own tourist page gives it, and so does the village's Wikipedia article, where the tree's picture is captioned simply "Linde von 1668". That makes it a little over 350 years old. It has grown to about twenty metres, and it has been a protected natural monument since 1984.

Put those two dates side by side. The neo-Romanesque church is not yet seventy years old; the tree was already close to three centuries old when it went up, and it was standing there when the church before it came down. On this square, the building is the thing that gets replaced and the lime is the thing that stays.

In 2020 the village added a small sculpture in its shade, the Steeklopper, a stone-breaker commemorating the local quarry trade. It is a good sign when a village keeps spending money on the ground around an old tree, and it gives the square a second reason to linger.

The sources say only "Linde", so we do not know whether this is a small-leaved, large-leaved or common lime. If you can tell from the leaves, let us know.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big lime, about twenty metres tall, on the square in front of St. Michael's Church, with the small Steeklopper stone-breaker sculpture in its shade.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the square hums with bees

name: Antoniusbaum

location.address: In the Sankt Vither Wald (St. Vith forest), Sankt-Vith, German-speaking Community of Belgium

access: Free, in the public St. Vith forest, described as a popular hiking destination; open at all times.
transport: In the St. Vith forest (Sankt Vither Wald); reached on foot via the forest's hiking paths, exact trailhead not confirmed this pass.
story:
This tree is known by the saint standing next to it. The Antoniusbaum takes its name from a statue of Saint Anthony beside it in the St. Vith forest, and it is the pairing, tree and saint together, that people walk out to see.

It is a named destination rather than a botanical record. In 1985 the German-speaking Community of Belgium put the Antoniusbaum area under landscape protection, which guards the setting as a whole rather than listing the trunk as a monumental tree. In 2007 the regional paper GrenzEcho reported the spot had been spruced up by private local initiative, and it is described as a popular goal for hikers in the Sankt Vither Wald.

That is close to everything on record, and we would rather say so than dress it up. No source we found names the species, gives an age or records a girth. The name is no help either: an Eiche or a Linde announces itself, an Anthony tree does not. A figure of "more than 300 years" circulates online, but we could not trace it to any page we trust, so it is not repeated here as fact.

What it offers is a walk through the forest to a place that people have kept tending, with a saint for company at the end. If you have stood under it and can say what kind of tree it is, or how big, tell us. You would be the first source.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the statue of Saint Anthony standing beside it, which gives the tree its name. It stands in the St. Vith forest, on the hiking paths of the Sankt Vither Wald.
